course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 2
unit.description: Follow the Spanish, French, Dutch, and British colonies, the regions of British North America, Atlantic trade, slavery, and colonial society from 1607 to 1754.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

questions.prompt: Spanish colonial institutions in the borderlands of North America were designed primarily to
choices: establish self-governing towns in which settlers and Native peoples shared political power equally
extract wealth, convert Native peoples to Christianity, and incorporate them into a ranked society
build trading posts that exchanged furs with Native nations without changing their religion
attract large numbers of Spanish farming families who would settle on land bought from Native peoples
questions.explanation: Spanish institutions subjugated Native peoples, converted them through missions, and incorporated them and Africans into colonial society.
choiceExplanations: Spain ruled through royal officials and a ranked society rather than shared power.
Spanish institutions subjugated Native peoples, converted them through missions, and incorporated them and Africans into colonial society.
Fur trading posts were the model of the French and Dutch, not the Spanish.
Few Spanish families settled in the borderlands, and land was not bought from Native peoples.
questions.distinguisher: Fur trading posts were a French and Dutch pattern, while Spain relied on missions and forced labor.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: French and Dutch colonial efforts in North America were similar in that both
choices: attracted large numbers of families who farmed land taken from American Indians and built permanent towns
forced American Indians to labor in silver mines under a system of tribute
banned trade with American Indians in order to protect settlers from conflict
involved relatively few Europeans and relied on trade alliances with American Indians for furs
questions.explanation: French and Dutch colonies had few settlers and relied on trade alliances and family ties with American Indians to acquire furs.
choiceExplanations: This describes the English colonies rather than the French and Dutch.
This describes Spanish colonies.
Both colonies depended on trade with Native peoples.
French and Dutch colonies had few settlers and relied on trade alliances and family ties with American Indians to acquire furs.
questions.distinguisher: Large farming settlements were an English pattern, which is why the near miss describes the wrong empire.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a difference between English colonization and French colonization in North America?
choices: English colonies attracted many families who farmed land taken from American Indians, while French colonies relied on trade
English colonies relied on fur-trading alliances with American Indians, while French colonies relied on farming families
English colonies were built mainly by missionaries, while French colonies were built mainly by soldiers
English colonies enslaved Native peoples through the encomienda, while French colonies used wage labor
questions.explanation: England sent many families who farmed and took land, while France built small colonies around the fur trade.
choiceExplanations: England sent many families who farmed and took land, while France built small colonies around the fur trade.
This reverses the two patterns.
Neither colony was built mainly by one group in this way.
The encomienda was a Spanish system.
questions.distinguisher: The near miss swaps the two colonial patterns.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why English colonization led to frequent conflict with American Indians over land?
choices: English colonists depended on Native partners for furs and therefore allied with them against Spain
English colonists were forbidden by the Crown to trade with American Indians, which led to hostility
English colonists focused on agriculture, took land from Native Americans, and lived apart from them
English colonists wanted to convert Native peoples to Anglicanism, and Native leaders refused all contact
questions.explanation: Farming colonists needed land, took it from Native peoples, and kept apart from them, which produced conflict over land.
choiceExplanations: Dependence on trade partners describes the French and Dutch, not English farm colonies.
English colonists did trade with American Indians, and the Crown did not forbid it.
Farming colonists needed land, took it from Native peoples, and kept apart from them, which produced conflict over land.
Conflict arose chiefly from land, and Native peoples did not refuse all contact.
questions.distinguisher: Trade-based colonies depended on Native partners, but English farming colonies needed Native land.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: The Dutch West India Company is best described as
choices: a religious order that sent missionaries to convert the Iroquois in the Hudson Valley
a royal army that conquered Native nations throughout New England on behalf of the Dutch crown
a Spanish agency that supplied enslaved labor for plantations in the West Indies
a private trading company that ran the Dutch colony of New Netherland and its fur trade
questions.explanation: The Dutch West India Company, a private company, governed New Netherland and organized its fur trade with Native nations.
choiceExplanations: The Dutch West India Company was a commercial enterprise, not a religious order.
It was a trading company and not a royal army.
It was a Dutch company, not a Spanish agency.
The Dutch West India Company, a private company, governed New Netherland and organized its fur trade with Native nations.
questions.distinguisher: Religious orders played a major role in New France, but the Dutch colony was organized as a business.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why Spain established missions in New Mexico?
choices: Spanish leaders sought to protect Native peoples from English colonists who were moving west
Spanish leaders sought to convert Native peoples and incorporate them into colonial society and labor
Spanish leaders sought to attract French fur traders who would develop the region's economy
Spanish leaders sought to build farming towns of free settlers who would pay taxes to the Crown
questions.explanation: Spain used missions to convert Native peoples to Christianity and to bring them into the colonial system.
choiceExplanations: Missions were established to convert Native peoples and secure Spanish control, not to protect them from the English.
Spain used missions to convert Native peoples to Christianity and to bring them into the colonial system.
Missions were not designed to attract French traders.
Spain built missions and presidios, and few free settlers farmed in the region.
questions.distinguisher: The Spanish did compete with other empires, but the missions served religious conversion and colonial control.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was the primary role of joint-stock companies in early English colonization?
choices: They provided military protection for colonies against Spanish and French forces
They granted Native peoples shares in colonial profits in exchange for the use of their land
They pooled the money of many investors to finance colonial ventures such as Jamestown
They managed colonial governments through elected assemblies in every English colony
questions.explanation: Investors pooled money in joint-stock companies, which spread the risk of expensive ventures such as the Virginia Company's Jamestown.
choiceExplanations: Joint-stock companies raised money; they were not armies.
Native peoples were not shareholders in these companies.
Investors pooled money in joint-stock companies, which spread the risk of expensive ventures such as the Virginia Company's Jamestown.
Companies financed ventures, and colonial assemblies developed separately.
questions.distinguisher: Some companies did govern colonies at first, but their main role was financing the venture.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why England was able to send larger numbers of migrants to North America than France or the Netherlands?
choices: The English Crown paid the full cost of every migrant's passage and set aside land for each family in advance
Spain had banned French and Dutch settlers from North America, leaving it open only to the English
English colonies offered the fur trade, which paid higher profits than the French or Dutch trade
Economic hardship and religious dissent at home, plus hope for land, pushed many English people to leave
questions.explanation: Many English people sought land, prosperity, and religious freedom, which pushed them toward colonies.
choiceExplanations: Most migrants paid their own way or came as indentured servants.
Spain did not ban French or Dutch settlement.
English colonies focused on agriculture rather than fur.
Many English people sought land, prosperity, and religious freedom, which pushed them toward colonies.
questions.distinguisher: The Crown did support colonization, but it did not pay for each migrant.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a specific historical development or process is situated within a broader historical context.

questions.prompt: Which of the following conclusions is best supported by the table?
choices: Spain established its settlements in North America only after England had founded its first colonies
Settlements founded for the fur trade outnumbered the settlements founded for any other single purpose
Empires founded settlements in North America for varied purposes, including defense, trade, and religion
Every English settlement in the table was founded by a group of English colonists seeking religious freedom
questions.explanation: The table lists military, commercial, governmental, missionary, and religious purposes across four empires.
choiceExplanations: St. Augustine, founded in 1565, came decades before Jamestown in 1607.
The table lists two trading posts and two settlements founded for religion, so trade does not outnumber the others.
The table lists military, commercial, governmental, missionary, and religious purposes across four empires.
Jamestown was founded to make a profit for investors.
questions.distinguisher: Religion explains Plymouth and Boston, but the table shows Jamestown was founded for profit, so the near miss overgeneralizes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a difference between the English settlements founded in 1620 and 1630 and the French and Dutch settlements shown in the table?
choices: The English settlements were founded as religious communities, while the French and Dutch settlements were founded as trading posts
The English settlements were founded as trading posts, while the French and Dutch settlements were founded as religious communities
The English settlements were founded to spread Catholicism, while the French and Dutch settlements were founded to spread Protestantism
The English settlements were founded to defend Spanish claims, while the French and Dutch settlements were founded for profit
questions.explanation: Plymouth and Boston were founded as religious communities, while Quebec and New Amsterdam were trading posts for the fur trade.
choiceExplanations: Plymouth and Boston were founded as religious communities, while Quebec and New Amsterdam were trading posts for the fur trade.
This reverses the purposes the table lists for each empire.
Plymouth and Boston were founded by Separatists and Puritans, who were Protestants, and Quebec and New Amsterdam were trading posts.
The table lists religious purposes for the 1620 and 1630 English settlements.
questions.distinguisher: The reversed statement uses the same two purposes, so you must check which empire the table assigns each one.

questions.prompt: The founding of Plymouth in 1620 and Boston in 1630 is best understood in the context of which of the following?
choices: Competition with the Dutch for control of the fur trade in the Hudson River valley
Spanish missions in New Mexico that threatened English access to the Atlantic coast
Parliament's Navigation Acts, which required English dissenters to settle in New England
Religious conflict in England that led dissenters to seek places where they could worship freely
questions.explanation: Separatists and Puritans left England because of religious conflict, and they founded Plymouth and Boston as religious communities.
choiceExplanations: The table lists religious purposes for Plymouth and Boston, and the Dutch fur trade was not their cause.
Santa Fe was far from New England and did not threaten English access to the coast.
The Navigation Acts began in 1651 and did not tell anyone where to settle.
Separatists and Puritans left England because of religious conflict, and they founded Plymouth and Boston as religious communities.
questions.distinguisher: The Dutch fur trade appears in the table, but it explains New Amsterdam rather than the English religious settlements.
